source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται.
pass_a_gloss: The things following must be given back and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy must be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not think that I am considering their allegories now as the gnosis delivers the truth, if they show something else, just like the ancient wise men, they indicate something else. But they say that God passes through all of existence, we however call Him only the Creator and the Creator by word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray, 'He passes through and fills all things because of His purity', since they did not understand that these things are said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not one principle. Let them know therefore that the so-called matter is without quality and without shape, as it is said in relation to them, and it is more daring to say that it does not exist in relation to Plato. And lest they know the one truly existing principle in the most mystical way in the Timaeus, he says these things in the same words. Now therefore let our position be as follows: the thing about all things, whether principle or principles or however it seems to them, is not to be spoken now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to explain the things that seem according to the present method. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed', has given them an opportunity for material existence. For Epicurus, the idea of spontaneity did not follow from what was said, hence vanity of vanities, all things are vanity. And Aristotle drew down providence to the moon from this psalm, 'Lord, your mercy and truth reach to the clouds'. For the explanation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been revealed before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire, and all the creative muse, but also Greek philosophy, were borrowed from barbarian philosophy. Plato indeed says in the last book of the Republic in the same words, 'Here therefore wild men, fiery to see, standing, learning the sound, having taken some privately, were leading, but having bound the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, having thrown and flayed, they were dragging along the road outside, striking on asphodels'. For the wild men, fiery, want to indicate angels to him, who having taken the unjust, punish them; He who makes, he says, His angels spirits and His servants a burning fire. It follows for them that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer.

pass_b_english: I must now return to the topics that follow and demonstrate more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics claim that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they claim the soul is; you will find all these assertions plainly stated in the scriptures. Do not suppose that I now treat their allegories as the gnosis delivers the truth, for if they point to something other than what they appear to say—much like the ancient wise wrestlers who feint one way and strike another—they signal a different meaning entirely. The Stoics say that God permeates all existence, but we call Him only the Creator, the Maker by His Word. The statement in Wisdom—‘He passes through and fills all things because of His purity’—misled them, since they failed to grasp that these words refer to the primal Wisdom created by God. They object that the philosophers—Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic alike—posit matter as a first principle, not a single one. Let them acknowledge, then, that this so-called matter is described by them as qualityless and formless, and even more boldly, that it does not exist according to Plato. And lest they claim to know the one truly existing principle in the most mystical sense from the Timaeus, he speaks in those very words. For now, let our position stand thus: the question concerning all things, whether there is one principle or many or whatever they suppose, is not to be discussed at present, for no other reason than the difficulty of explaining what appears plausible by our current method. Besides, the prophetic utterance, ‘the earth was invisible and unformed,’ gave them an opening for the notion of material substance. Epicurus, failing to follow the sense of the text, let the idea of chance slip in, ending in ‘vanity of vanities, all is vanity.’ Aristotle, drawing providence down only as far as the moon from the psalm ‘Lord, your mercy is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds’ (Psalm 36:5), did so because the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet come before the Lord’s advent. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire were borrowed from barbarian philosophy by the entire poetic tradition and by Greek philosophy itself. Plato, in the final book of the Republic, says in these very words: ‘Here wild men, fiery to behold, stand by, discerning the sound; taking some aside privately they lead them away, but binding the hands, feet, and head of Aridaeus and the others, throwing them down and flaying them, they drag them along the road outside, striking them on asphodels.’ The fiery wild men, he says, represent angels who seize the wicked to punish them—‘He who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire.’ It follows for them that the soul is immortal, for what is punished or instructed while possessing sensation lives on, even if it is said to suffer.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex arguments regarding the origins of Greek philosophical concepts (matter, providence, the soul) and their relationship to scripture and barbarian philosophy. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Greek, while Pass B provides a more fluent rendering that remains faithful to the source. Scripture citations (Psalm 36:5) are correctly identified and applied to the quoted text. The translation of 'ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον' as 'without quality and without shape' is faithful to the Greek. The description of the Republic passage is complete.
Stählin, GCS Clemens Alexandrinus II (1906), via Perseus canonical-greekLit TEI (local copy, perseus-grc2)
